section_title: What happens when Saul meets the Jesus he is opposing?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the disciples of the Lord. He approached the high priest 2 and requested letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any men or women belonging to the Way, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

3 As Saul drew near to Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” 5 “Who are You, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He replied. 6 “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” 7 The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless. They heard the voice but did not see anyone. 8 Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could not see a thing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus. 9 For three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything.

context_lines: Saul is still threatening the disciples when he requests letters to the synagogues in Damascus. His aim is to arrest men and women belonging to the Way and bring them to Jerusalem. The Way is a name for the followers of Jesus; the people Saul seeks are the same community he has been attacking.

Near Damascus, a light from heaven interrupts the journey. Saul falls to the ground and hears Jesus identify Himself as the One Saul is persecuting. Saul has been attacking disciples, yet Jesus speaks of those attacks as directed against Himself. He orders Saul into the city to await further instructions.

The man who came to take others away as prisoners now has to be led by the hand. For three days he cannot see and takes neither food nor drink. Luke describes an encounter with the risen Jesus, followed by helplessness and waiting, before introducing Ananias.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians read this as an act of mercy initiated by Jesus, who confronts a persecutor rather than waiting for him to become friendly to the faith. They differ over how this striking account relates to God’s grace and human response in conversion more generally.

The Reformed [Westminster Confession, chapter 10, paragraphs 1–2](https://www.opc.org/wcf.html), teaches that God renews the will of those He has chosen and brings them to Christ, so that they come freely because His grace makes them willing. [Calvin on verse 3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/acts/9.htm) emphasizes the reversal of Saul’s hostile purpose.

The Methodist [Articles of Religion, Article VIII](https://www.umc.org/en/content/articles-of-religion), teach that people cannot turn to faith by their own natural strength: God’s grace goes before them and works with their response. [Wesley on verse 15](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-acts-of-the-apostles/) distinguishes God’s unconditional selection of particular people for particular work from the broader questions readers may ask about salvation.

The Catholic Church’s [Catechism, paragraphs 153–155](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_one/section_one/chapter_three/article_1/iii_the_characteristics_of_faith.index.html), likewise calls faith God’s gift while describing believing as a human act in which the mind and will cooperate with grace. These statements give different frameworks for understanding God’s action; none makes Saul the person who first sought this meeting with Jesus.

The later accounts add details. [Acts 22:9](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/22.htm), in the BSB, says the companions could not understand the voice, while verse 7 here says they heard it. [Acts 26:13–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/26.htm) describes the light and says they all fell. Luke’s accounts should be compared rather than filling this scene with details it does not give, such as a horse.
god_plan_lines: Jesus’ identification with the people Saul attacks is a powerful part of the encounter. A related connection appears in [1 Corinthians 12:12–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/12.htm), where Paul describes believers as Christ’s body and explains that one member’s suffering concerns the others. This is a biblical connection, not a claim that this scene contains every later detail of Paul’s teaching about the church.

Paul later explains the mercy shown to him in [1 Timothy 1:12–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_timothy/1.htm): his former violence becomes the background against which Christ’s patience is displayed for others who will believe. His past is not denied or excused. It does not prevent Christ from showing mercy and appointing him to service.
current_position_lines: Returning to the Word draws on the name “the Way” in this passage to describe a life rooted in Jesus and grounded in what God has said. Following Him involves a way of living, not simply adopting a religious label. This is the study’s developed point about the name; it does not settle the separate questions about how every conversion takes place.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Returning to the Word — The Way; directly develops Acts 9:2,19:9,24:14 as the site’s call to a life rooted in Christ and Scripture. Limited to this point, not a new position on grace and free will.
